blocks.body:
Hash Store is a mobile app that primarily sells technology accessories. The interviewer provided a short scenario for purchasing computer accessories online with a straightforward payment method.



The goal was to create a clean, simple checkout experience for someone buying a camera setup for videos and remote meetings.



I used the Double Diamond model, starting with secondary research and then narrowing the work around payment and checkout friction.
blocks.heading: About the project

blocks.caption: Hash Store mobile app concept
blocks.alt: Hash Store mobile commerce project overview

blocks.body:
Because time was limited, I used secondary research to study common checkout problems and real user reviews. The main issues were complex account creation, unclear shipping options, weak card-field implementation, hidden fees, long checkout flows, and having to restart after an error.



I grouped the findings in an affinity map and focused the project on payment friction. A persona and user story helped keep the design grounded: as a TikTok user, Noha wants to order mobile accessories using different payment methods so she can improve her video setup.



I compared Noon, Amazon, and Jumia, concentrating on checkout and payment features. The resulting problem statement was simple: Noha needs to buy a ring light and tripod online with flexible payment options and a straightforward checkout process.

blocks.body:
The information architecture translated the research into a simpler purchase path. I mapped the product-selection and checkout user flow, then moved from quick paper sketches into digital wireframes.



The high-fidelity work began with three onboarding screens that introduced the app’s key features. The home experience combined promotional banners, categories, recommendations, and a shopping cart with a clear cost breakdown.



Checkout offered delivery or pickup, address details, and delivery preferences. Payment options included cash, bank cards, PayPal, e-wallets, and crypto. A final order-review step let users confirm everything before placing the order.

blocks.body:
I ran a remote moderated usability study focused on checkout time, drop-off points, and cart abandonment. The main findings were that users could not change the language and had no place to apply a discount. The first iteration added a promo-code field to the payment screen.



The interviewer also highlighted that no payment option had a default state and asked how the experience supported the business goal of promoting its crypto-payment gateway. That feedback showed me the importance of balancing user needs with commercial priorities.



I also learned to keep the core user goal visible throughout the process and to spend more time validating the color system before moving into final UI.
